deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler's 'Tractatus de numerorum doctrina' (E792), Cap. 3, on the divisor sum. Euler writes the divisor sum as a long-s ∫N; here it is σ(N). The page has four parts.

(a) End of §101: the values σ(N) for N = 1..60 come from the table in §100. Since σ(N) ≥ N+1 for N > 1, every value ≤ 60 comes from some N ≤ 59, so this table is complete for values up to 60.
- Values in 1..60 that never occur as σ(N): 2, 5, 9, 10, 11, 16, 17, 19, 21, 22, 23, 25, 26, 27, 29, 33, 34, 35, 37, 41, 43, 45, 46, 47, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 55, 58, 59 (32 numbers).
- Values that do occur: 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, 15, 18, 20, 24, 28, 30, 31, 32, 36, 38, 39, 40, 42, 44, 48, 54, 56, 57, 60 (28 numbers).

(b) §102: σ is not injective. Every repeated value ≤ 60 is listed:
- σ(6)=σ(11)=12
- σ(10)=σ(17)=18
- σ(16)=σ(25)=31
- σ(21)=σ(31)=32
- σ(34)=σ(53)=54
- σ(28)=σ(39)=56
- σ(14)=σ(15)=σ(23)=24
- σ(20)=σ(26)=σ(41)=42
- σ(33)=σ(35)=σ(47)=48
- σ(24)=σ(38)=σ(59)=60

(c) §§103–105: the abundancy problem. Find N with σ(N)/N = m/n.
- Since σ(N) ≥ N+1 for N > 1, one needs m > n; m = n forces N = 1.
- §104. Take gcd(m,n) = 1. From nσ(N) = mN we get n | N (this step is implicit; mine). Write N = an. Then σ(an) = am.
- Lemma (from §§97–99): for a > 1, σ(an) > aσ(n). Reason: the divisors a·d (d | n) contribute aσ(n), and the divisor 1 of an is not of that form. Hence a > 1 implies m > σ(n).
- Consequences:
  - m < σ(n): no solution.
  - m = σ(n): the unique solution is N = n.
  - m > σ(n): any solution has the form N = an with a > 1, but a solution need not exist.
- §105 restates this and asserts, without example, that ratios with m > σ(n) and no solution exist.
- Modern reading: if gcd(n, σ(n)) = 1, then n is the only number with abundancy σ(n)/n, i.e. n is 'solitary'.

(d) §§106–108: even perfect numbers, σ(N) = 2N.
- Write N = 2^n·A with A odd and n ≥ 1. Then σ(N) = (2^{n+1}−1)σ(A) = 2^{n+1}A, so σ(A)/A = 2^{n+1}/(2^{n+1}−1).
- §107. This fraction is in lowest terms. Apply §104 with denominator M = 2^{n+1}−1 and numerator M+1.
- Since σ(M) ≥ M+1, the case σ(M) > M+1 gives no solution. The case σ(M) = M+1 holds exactly when M is prime, and then A = M.
- Hence N = 2^n(2^{n+1}−1) with 2^{n+1}−1 prime.
- §108 adds:
  - 2^{n+1}−1 can be prime only if n+1 is prime, but not conversely.
  - Whether odd perfect numbers exist has not been decided.

(e) §109, begun here: suppose N = ABCD… is an odd perfect number (A, B, … implicitly prime powers). Then σ(A)σ(B)σ(C)σ(D) = 2ABCD, which is singly even ('impariter par'). The next page concludes that exactly one σ-factor is ≡ 2 mod 4. This gives Euler's form (4k+1)^{4λ+1}P^2.
errors: No mathematical errors found. All 60 σ-values behind the lists, both lists, and all ten coincidence groups check out; the coincidence list is complete for values ≤ 60.
Implicit step (§104): n | N follows from nσ(N) = mN with gcd(m,n) = 1. Euler states it without proof.

§105: Euler asserts, without any example, that some ratios with m > σ(n) admit no solution. This is true but unproved here; explicit examples were only supplied in the modern abundancy-index literature, as far as I know.
§106 wording: 'ipso duplo est major' is to be read as 'is twice as large as itself', i.e. σ(N) = 2N, as the next sentence makes explicit.
§107 uses that σ(A)/A in lowest terms has numerator and denominator M+1 and M. It also implicitly uses n ≥ 1 (so M > 1). Both are fine.

results.what: Table of numbers ≤ 60 that are / are not values of σ, and multiplicities of σ-values
results.modern_name: Non-totient-type data for σ: 'non-sigma' numbers (OEIS A007369) and σ-collisions (A007370 etc.)

results.what: If σ(N)/N = m/n in lowest terms, then N = an and σ(an) ≥ aσ(n) with equality iff a = 1. So no solution if m < σ(n), and a unique solution N = n if m = σ(n).
results.modern_name: Abundancy index; criterion that gcd(n, σ(n)) = 1 implies n is solitary; non-index criterion n < m < σ(n)
results.usually_credited_to: Solitary/friendly terminology: Anderson & Hickerson (1977). Non-index criterion: often cited from Weiner / Holdener (2000s). The gcd criterion is folklore.

results.what: Every even perfect number is 2^n(2^{n+1}−1) with 2^{n+1}−1 prime; this requires n+1 prime
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (posthumous, 1849: De numeris amicabilibus and this Tractatus)

results.what: Start of the argument that an odd perfect number has the form p^{4λ+1}·P^2 with p ≡ 1 mod 4
results.modern_name: Euler's theorem on the form of odd perfect numbers

deep.surprise_reason: The perfect-number material is Euler's well-known proof from this already-published (1849) treatise. The only mildly notable item is §104: Euler has, in effect, the sufficient condition gcd(n,σ(n)) = 1 ⇒ n solitary, and the non-index criterion n < m < σ(n). These are usually cited from 20th-century literature, but they are elementary and the text is well known.
